items.prompt: In the roofline model, what determines whether a kernel is memory-bound or compute-bound?
choices: Its parameter count
Its arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte moved) relative to the machine's ridge point
The number of GPU streaming multiprocessors used
Whether it uses floating-point or integer arithmetic
items.explain: Attainable throughput is min(peak compute, bandwidth × intensity); kernels below the ridge point's intensity are limited by memory bandwidth.

items.prompt: Why is batch-1 autoregressive decoding of a large LLM usually memory-bound?
choices: Each new token rereads all weights (and the KV cache) while doing only a few FLOPs per byte
Each token needs a full backward pass
Softmax cannot run on tensor cores
The tokenizer runs on the CPU
items.explain: Generating one token multiplies vectors by every weight matrix once, so bytes moved dominate FLOPs and intensity is low.

items.prompt: What does FlashAttention mainly reduce to obtain its speedup?
choices: The number of FLOPs in attention
The number of attention heads
The precision of the attention scores
Reads and writes between GPU HBM and on-chip SRAM
items.explain: It tiles the computation in SRAM and never materializes the N×N score matrix in HBM; FLOPs stay quadratic.

items.prompt: Compared with standard softmax attention, FlashAttention's output is:
choices: An approximation with bounded error controlled by a rank parameter
A sparse attention restricted to local windows
The same exact attention, up to floating-point rounding from a different summation order
A linear-attention approximation using kernel features
items.explain: Tiling with a running max and normalizer rearranges the same sums, so the result is exact in real arithmetic.

items.prompt: How does KV-cache memory for one sequence scale during decoding with standard attention?
choices: Constant in sequence length
Linearly in the number of tokens so far
Quadratically in the number of tokens so far
Logarithmically in the number of tokens so far
items.explain: Each token adds one key and one value vector per layer and KV head, so memory grows linearly with context.

items.prompt: What does PagedAttention change about the KV cache?
choices: It stores the cache in fixed-size blocks so memory is allocated without fragmentation and prefixes can be shared
It compresses keys and values to 2 bits
It evicts old tokens to keep memory constant
It recomputes keys and values instead of storing them
items.explain: Inspired by virtual-memory paging, it changes allocation and sharing, not the amount of state per token.

items.prompt: What is iteration-level (continuous) batching?
choices: Waiting until a full batch of requests arrives before starting
Batching only the attention operations
Running each request on a separate GPU
Rescheduling the batch every decoding step so finished sequences leave and new ones join
items.explain: Orca schedules at the granularity of one model iteration rather than whole requests.

items.prompt: Why does batching more sequences raise decoding throughput on a GPU?
choices: It reduces the number of layers
It shortens every sequence
It lets one read of each weight serve many sequences, raising arithmetic intensity
It removes the need for a KV cache
items.explain: Decode is memory-bound; reusing each weight read across the batch moves it toward the compute roof, until KV memory or latency limits are hit.

items.prompt: What did StreamingLLM find about window attention that keeps only the most recent tokens?
choices: It works perfectly at any length
It fails once text exceeds the cache, but keeping a few initial “attention sink” tokens largely restores it
It is slower than full attention
It requires retraining the model from scratch
items.explain: Initial tokens receive large attention scores as sinks; keeping their KV plus a recent window stabilizes long streaming.

items.prompt: A model with an attention-sink plus sliding-window cache keeps stable perplexity over 1 million tokens. What does this NOT show?
choices: That the model can recall a fact from far outside the kept window
That memory use is bounded
That decoding speed is roughly constant per token
That the cache size is fixed
items.explain: Evicted tokens are gone; stable perplexity does not mean long-range retrieval works.

items.prompt: According to Sardana et al., how does large expected inference demand change the cost-optimal model?
choices: Train a larger model on fewer tokens
Inference demand does not change the optimum
Use only mixture-of-experts models
Train a smaller model on more tokens than Chinchilla-optimal
items.explain: Adding lifetime inference cost to the objective favors smaller models that are cheaper per query, trained longer.

items.prompt: What did Luccioni et al. find when measuring the energy of 1,000 inferences across model types?
choices: Task-specific models used more energy than general-purpose ones
All models used about the same energy
Multi-purpose generative models were orders of magnitude more expensive than task-specific ones, even at matched parameter count
Energy depended only on parameter count
items.explain: Generality came at a steep energy cost per inference in their comparison.

items.prompt: What problem does LLM.int8 address with its mixed-precision decomposition?
choices: Slow tokenization
Outlier feature dimensions with large magnitudes that break naive 8-bit quantization
Vanishing gradients during training
Too many attention heads
items.explain: It keeps the few outlier dimensions in 16-bit and quantizes the rest to 8-bit.

items.prompt: A 4-bit model shows only a 0.1 perplexity increase over FP16. Which conclusion is safest?
choices: The average loss is small, but specific capabilities, long contexts or rare inputs may still degrade and need separate evaluation
All capabilities are preserved
The model will be exactly 4× faster at every batch size
The KV cache is now 4× smaller
items.explain: Averages can hide concentrated damage; speedups need kernels, and weight quantization alone does not shrink the KV cache.

items.prompt: In speculative sampling, a drafted token x is accepted with probability:
choices: q(x)
p(x) · q(x)
Always 1 if the draft is greedy
min(1, p(x)/q(x)), where p is the target and q the draft distribution
items.explain: On rejection, the token is resampled from the normalized residual max(0, p − q); this makes the output exactly distributed as p.

items.prompt: If the draft model in speculative sampling is poorly matched to the target, what happens?
choices: Outputs follow the draft distribution
The method fails and returns errors
Outputs still follow the target distribution, but fewer tokens are accepted, so the speedup falls
Outputs become greedy
items.explain: Exactness holds for any draft under the acceptance rule; only efficiency depends on agreement.

items.prompt: In Hinton et al.'s distillation, what is a “soft target”?
choices: A label smoothed with uniform noise
The teacher's output distribution computed with a raised softmax temperature
A target that the student may ignore
The average of all training labels
items.explain: Raising the temperature exposes the teacher's relative probabilities over incorrect classes.

items.prompt: Minimizing soft-target cross-entropy H(p_T, q) over student distributions q is equivalent to minimizing:
choices: KL(p_T ‖ q), since H(p_T, q) = H(p_T) + KL(p_T ‖ q) and H(p_T) is fixed
KL(q ‖ p_T)
The squared error between logits only
The entropy of q
items.explain: The teacher's entropy is constant, so cross-entropy and forward KL share their minimizer, q = p_T when the student can represent it.

items.prompt: What does the lottery-ticket hypothesis claim?
choices: Random pruning always improves accuracy
Only the largest weights matter at initialization
Pruned networks never need retraining
Dense networks contain sparse subnetworks that, reset to their original initialization, train in isolation to comparable accuracy
items.explain: Iterative magnitude pruning found such subnetworks at 10–20% of original size on small vision networks.

items.prompt: Why does 90% unstructured weight sparsity often give little speedup on a GPU?
choices: Sparse weights use more memory
GPUs cannot store zeros
Irregular sparsity does not map to dense matrix hardware without special kernels or hardware support
Pruning increases FLOPs
items.explain: Structured pruning (channels, heads, layers) or sparse kernels are needed to turn sparsity into speed.

items.prompt: In a Switch Transformer layer, each token is processed by:
choices: Every expert, averaged
One expert selected by a learned router
A random expert
The attention layer only
items.explain: Top-1 routing keeps FLOPs per token constant while total parameters grow with the number of experts.

items.prompt: A mixture-of-experts model has 8× the parameters of a dense model at the same FLOPs per token. Which cost does NOT stay the same?
choices: Memory to store the weights
Arithmetic per token
Number of attention heads
Vocabulary size
items.explain: All experts must be stored and moved, so memory and communication grow even though per-token FLOPs do not.

items.prompt: What does LoRA train?
choices: All weights at reduced precision
Only the embedding layer
A new attention head per layer
A low-rank update ΔW = BA added to frozen pretrained weights
items.explain: The pretrained weights stay frozen; only the small factors B and A are learned, and they can be merged for inference.

items.prompt: Biderman et al. compared LoRA with full fine-tuning on code and maths. What did they find?
choices: LoRA matched full fine-tuning everywhere
LoRA forgot more and learned more
LoRA learned less on the target domain but forgot less outside it
Full fine-tuning learned only low-rank updates
items.explain: Full fine-tuning learned updates of 10–100× higher rank than typical LoRA settings.

items.prompt: What did Hoffmann et al. (Chinchilla) conclude about compute-optimal training?
choices: Model size should grow much faster than data
Parameters and training tokens should be scaled in roughly equal proportion
Data matters more than parameters at every scale
Loss stops improving beyond 10B parameters
items.explain: Chinchilla, with 70B parameters and 1.4T tokens, beat the 280B Gopher at the same training compute.

items.prompt: Why is a “compute-optimal” model not necessarily the cheapest model to deploy?
choices: Compute-optimal counts training FLOPs only; with heavy inference use, a smaller model trained longer can cost less overall
Scaling laws are exact
Larger models always run faster
Compute-optimal models cannot be quantized
items.explain: Inference cost scales with model size and query volume, which the training-only optimum ignores.

items.prompt: In Snell et al.'s FLOPs-matched comparison, when could test-time compute beat a 14× larger model?
choices: On every problem
Only on the hardest problems
Only with greedy decoding
On problems where the smaller model already had somewhat non-trivial success
items.explain: On the hardest problems, extra pretraining was more effective than test-time search.

items.prompt: A compressed state has discarded a fact needed to answer a question. What can more test-time compute on that state achieve?
choices: Recover the fact by reasoning longer
Recover it if best-of-n is used
Not recover it: processing cannot add information the state lost, though it can extract more from what was kept
Recover it by lowering temperature
items.explain: Shannon information cannot grow by processing (data processing inequality); computation can raise usable information only from what remains.

items.prompt: What happens to the gold reward as n grows when best-of-n selects against an imperfect proxy reward model?
choices: It rises without limit
It rises at first, then falls, as selection finds candidates the proxy overrates
It stays constant
It falls from the start
items.explain: Gao et al. observed this overoptimization in a synthetic setup with a larger reward model as gold.

items.prompt: The often-quoted KL(best-of-n ‖ reference) = log n − (n−1)/n is, according to Beirami et al.:
choices: An upper bound on the actual KL divergence
Exact for every reward function
A lower bound on the actual KL divergence
Only valid for n = 2
items.explain: They disprove the equality, show it is an upper bound, and propose a tighter estimator.

items.prompt: How does Inference-Time Intervention (ITI) change a model's behaviour?
choices: By fine-tuning all weights on truthful data
By filtering outputs with a separate classifier
By changing the tokenizer
By shifting activations along learned directions in a few attention heads during decoding
items.explain: ITI raised Alpaca's TruthfulQA truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1% without weight updates.

items.prompt: For the alignment thesis, what must an inference-time correction show before it counts as a correction actuator?
choices: A large effect on one benchmark
That it needs no labelled data
That its effect persists, unrelated capabilities hold on independent evaluations, and it sits outside the model's write access
That it lowers latency
items.explain: The thesis asks for persistent, measured corrections without silent damage to unrelated capability.
